## 2. Audiences don’t understand camp. Two recent examples being Masters of the Universe and Stop! That! Train!

**Score:** 802
**Body:** I genuinely think audiences have forgotten how to understand/appreciate camp, and it’s robbing people of the ability to enjoy movies that are being extremely clever and funny on purpose. Everything gets judged by the same weird standard of realism and sincerity now. If something is heightened, ridiculous, aggressively theatrical, or knowingly stupid, people treat it like the filmmakers accidentally made a bad movie instead of considering that maybe the absurdity is the entire point.

*Masters of the Universe* and *Stop That Train!* are two recent examples that made this especially obvious to me. Both understand exactly what kind of movie they are making and commit to the bit, which is what makes them so fun. I can’t think of a better moment in cinematic history than “THE BRAKES ARE FRIED” and then a sudden cut to train brakes…covered in breading and frying in oil??? I think about this daily. 

Are there any other movies that come to mind that were either received poorly or didn’t get the accolades they deserved?

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Why does The Sopranos have such an unusually deep cast of characters?

**Score:** 187
**Body:** One thing that always strikes me about The Sopranos is that its strength isn't just in the writing of the main story, but in how many of its characters are genuinely memorable and well-developed.

A lot of them initially seem almost like simple archetypes or one-trick characters. Paulie seems like the superstitious old-school guy, Silvio seems like the calm consigliere, Christopher seems like the impulsive young gangster, Junior seems like the bitter old uncle, Ralphie seems like the completely unhinged psychopath, etc.

But as the series progresses, you realize that these characters aren't really defined by just those traits. They have contradictions, insecurities, relationships, histories, and moments that reveal sides of them you weren't necessarily expecting. Yet they still remain recognizably themselves rather than feeling like the writers simply changed their personalities for the sake of development.

What do you think makes The Sopranos so good at this? Is it the writing, the acting, the amount of time the show gives its characters, the way they interact with each other, or something more fundamental about how the show approaches characterization?

And are there other films or TV shows that you think achieve this same kind of character depth across such a large ensemble?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. After the fast paced first season, the show becomes far less plot heavy and far more character study driven. Plot is still happening but more incrementally, sometimes almost in the background, and the bulk of the time is spent on exploring all of the many flavors of fucked up these people are

(This is partly because the first season covered all of the plot of David Chase’s original idea for a movie. That had all been worked out already, the rest of the show was more winging it in comparison)
2. David Chase had over 25 years experience in writing and producing TV before he created the show and he set a very high bar for what he wanted. The writers room was bursting with talent, including the future creators of Mad Men and Boardwalk Empire. As the show found it's feet, the actors had the time and space to really sink into their characters and give rich performances. Being on HBO helped because the culture there favoured prestige and quality rather than only focusing on viewing figures. HBO also stuck with one of my all time favorite shows "The Larry Sanders Show" even though viewing figures were extremely modest compared to big network tv comedies like Friends and Seinfeld. Taking a risk on people who want to create high art can pay off. 
  - Plus, at that point in HBO's history, the writers' room was deeply respected as their main source of quality content, with almost no executive producer interference. I don't how it is now, but a lot was written about the subject back then. It's how we got great stuff like The Wire


  - Music choices too.

This show got me started with Van Morrison which has been as life changing as the sopranos was
    - I love Van Morrison but haven't watched much Sopranos. Which track is featured? 
3. SPOILERS IN THIS COMMENT

I think it's because they managed to recreate something about the human experience which is very close to real life - it was something many people recognised from their own lived experience. It's difficult to talk about, because at its root it communicates the suspicion that human beings are ultimately unknowable, and they're unknowable most of all to themselves. 

The Sopranos excelled at multiple motivations - there was never just one reason a character did the thing, there were 2 or 3 or 4 reasons, and maybe a couple of reasons actually contradicted each other. So motivations were fuzzy, and yet the action itself was utterly convincing. We believed that character would do that thing, and we could make intelligent guesses as to why, but we could never be absolutely sure. The classic example is Tony killing Ralph; an endless source of debate within the Sopranos fandom. This feeling of believability coupled with ambiguity is just so real. It's how many of us experience life. 

Furthermore, The Sopranos understood that contradictory motivations can be equally sincere. So Tony calls his cousin, Tony B, and during the call confesses a great secret that has created a distance between them for many years. The phone call is healing for both. But the phone call is also a means for Tony to track Tony B's location; information he knows will lead to his cousin's death. The call had to be of a certain length for the location to be affirmed, Tony had to keep Tony B on the phone for a certain amount of time. It was a trap. But Tony's confession was utterly sincere. The healing was real, and the ulterior motive did not detract from it. 

The Sopranos understood that a human being is not one entity, that many people can inhabit one body and they can act independently and both actions can be authentic. And beneath that is the inevitable, horrifying possibility that the real reason the character did the thing, the real reason any of us do any of the things we do, is because we want to. It begins with the impulse to do the thing, and anything more complicated than that gets filled in later, either by ourselves or by others as rationalisations in retrospect. Tony killed Ralph because he wanted to, and you can end the debate there and you will be closer to the truth than hours of debate about horses and strippers will ever get you. 

I've seldom seen drama, on TV or otherwise, that more accurately describes something so real about the human condition.
4. Of course a lot of this is just writing and acting, but a lot of it is also the unique production philosophy of early HBO.

Part of the secret to that era, it seems to me, is just that there seems to be much less of the jockeying for cast position that you see on network shows. Not every main character needs to appear in every episode, not every main character needs to have some big character arc spanning a season. Conversely, they stocked a really *really* deep cast bench, so there’s a lot of guys whose role for much of the show is just to fill crowd scenes, but they’re played by great actors and can carry an episode when the story needs them. They seed some plotlines for those characters years and years in advance. So the social world seems a little less rigid and more naturalistic.

Those shows were also very good at keeping minor characters in play. Consider Barbara, the third Soprano sister who shows up once every season or so, and never has a huge role. A network show would likely get that actress on for a guest spot and then “lose” her, and either have to recast her or just work around the character for the rest of the show. Sopranos almost never seemed to have that problem.

When you have a good *big* cast and good writing, the effect on the main characters is multiplicative. Tony really feels like he has a social and family life as big and complex as a normal person’s. You meet his *extended* family, all the friends he made in 40 - 50 years of life, his *entire* professional network, and his friends’ and colleagues‘ families, and all of these characters feel like real people with their own lives. It doesn’t just feel like the strictly hemmed-in life of a normal TV character, where you’re told which people are important and who to focus on. It’s all that context that allows Tony to feel like such a complete person.

Sopranos is a really special show, but a lot of what I said also applies to The Wire and (my personal favorite) Deadwood.
  - Funnily enough, they actually did recast Barbara, lol
  - Oh, and Sopranos—and this partly comes down to it being one of the first shows that was reliably available on home video; every Blockbuster had the set—also isn’t always *reminding* you of things in the way that a network show is. It assumes you remember the characters’ history as well as the characters do.

A moment that really strikes me is in season 5 when Tony is contemplating what to do about Feech La Manna. And Tony shouts “have I learned nothing from Richie Aprile?” A character who died three years ago. He doesn’t elaborate at all. We’re put in the position of thinking back to that years-old plotline and knowing what Tony means by that.

An earlier show would *never* put that line in, because they assume the viewer wouldn’t know or wouldn’t remember what Tony’s talking about. But because Sopranos can put it in, we see that Tony is a full person who has the whole history of his life guiding his every action.
5. It is all of the above. It was 6 seasons devoted primarily to the characters and their interactions with one another. Tony was one of the first anti heroes on TV, and a lot made him so relatable was his relationships with all his family members. Additionally, the idea of therapy and the dream sequences were quite brilliant as it allowed a real peak into Tony’s psyche. All of this works largely because of how brilliant James Gandolfini was. Go look at just his breathing in the show; this is basically a character in its own right. 

Furthermore, the show got to make such excellent characters because it treated the audience with a lot of respect. Look at this scene (spoilers ahead) https://youtu.be/X8LVP0wOI5g?is=WUvwDjdVQsAu60MN . Look how much this says about Chris in 40 seconds, with no dialogue. Imagine if they had to spell this out for you; the show begins to fall apart quickly. 

So all in all, I think it is everything you said. It is incredibly well written, well acted, and there isn’t too much plot besides character interactions. It is largely considered the greatest show for a reason. 

## 2. First Viewing of The Truman Show

**Score:** 23
**Body:** Finally watched *The Truman Show* last night. I went in expecting to like it given my love for Peter Weir as the director of *Witness* and *Master and Commander*, but I was still amazed how much I loved this. The premise of a man who's whole life has been a TV show is honestly frightening and the writer Andrew Niccol manages to walk a fine line between comedy, drama, and even touches of horror in depicting Truman Burbank's life which has been completely made up. Yet, it's also an uplifting film in showing the curiosity of man and what one will do to achieve a new life. It also has one of the most memorable settings ever with the Island and the cinematography by Peter Biziou is brilliant in making everything appear like a Reality TV show, particularly during the shots of stationary cameras.

And of course, Jim Carrey. Having recently gotten into some of his films, I have to say this is easily his performance I've seen yet. Still has moments of his traditional comedic charm, but manages to have some genuinely heartfelt scenes where he really says so much without a lot of dialogue. If ever there was a film that proved Carrey could be a dramatic actor when he chose to, *The Truman Show* is certainly that film. 

From the many comedies I've seen, *The Truman Show* is most definitely one of the most original while also having something to say about living in the real world. Easily the magnum opus of Peter Weir's filmography.

## 3. The Cremaster Cycle makes a lot more sense once you stop treating them as films

**Score:** 14
**Body:** Saw all five over three nights years ago at a repertory screening, in the order they were made rather than numerical order, which I'd recommend if you ever get the chance.

Going in I had basically no art background. I'd seen the Guggenheim show in 2002 and mostly remembered it as very expensive and very sticky. So a lot of the first night was me sitting there watching a guy in goat prosthetics tap dance on a pier while two drag racers circle an island in opposite directions, wondering what exactly I had signed up for. There's also a bit where they try to install a tire with Truck Nutz on it. I laughed out loud, but nobody joined in.

The thing that flipped it for me happened on night three. I stopped trying to follow them as narratives and started noticing the patterns across the cycle. Feet. Women's shoes specifically, or things attached to shoes. The way locations invert: Old World, New World, both, New, Old. Once you've seen all of them the repetitions start doing the work that plot normally does.

Which got me to what I actually think about Barney. He went to school for this stuff and so did I, sort of (NYU Tisch School of the Arts, Dramatic Writing), and there are really only two dramatic structures anybody uses. Aristotelian rising and falling action, which is almost everything, and Brechtian, which is Brecht and a bit of Mamet. Barney isn't working in either. He's building the structure itself and then filling it with film, sculpture, performance, whatever. The films are an output of the structure. They're not the point.

Anyway that reframe made the whole thing tolerable and occasionally great. Cremaster 2 is the one I'd point a newcomer to. It's the closest to a real story, the Gilmore material gives it a spine, and Norman Mailer plays Houdini, which is a sentence I enjoy typing.

I did not make it to the end of Cremaster 3. Three hours, that soundtrack, on night three of this. I knew how it ended because I'd seen the Guggenheim installation. Left with about an hour to go. Still a little annoyed about it, honestly, though less every year.

I could be wrong about the structure thing. Curious whether people who know his work better read it the same way.

I agree with your idea of not treating them as "films". Barney as an artist is a lot more interesting and capable than he is as a director. Thats not to mean I think the Cremaster Cycle is bad. There's just a lot of moments in his works where a better director could do something technically better. But as epic art pieces? They are absolutely gorgeous and enthralling. Especially 2 and 3. 
2. I saw these maybe 25 years ago at the MFAH, all in a single day. What a fucking day. Have been wanting to see them again ever since. There has not quite been a lot of other art that has made me think about it for as long as I have this. At this point it's been so long I can only really remember bits and pieces. At the time I remember just thinking what in the absolute fuck does any of this have to do with the nut muscle? 
3. I think you’re spot on about the structure. To the structure I’d add that it’s also about the dynamics between parts of the structure(s). Push, pull, tension, release, fullness, emptiness, etc. The structures are living dynamic systems and you only ever see parts of them from one perspective or another. At least that’s my take

**Body:** On the surface it begins almost like a simple memory of youth and first love, but gradually the reality around Erik starts breaking down. Places empty out, people seem to change roles, memories contradict one another, and he becomes increasingly unsure of where he is, or even what exactly he is remembering.

The film plays with memory, identity, masculinity, love, death and the question of whether a life has a predetermined purpose. I deliberately wanted the audience to construct an explanation before the film gives them enough information to know whether they’re right.

One of the ideas underneath it is that perhaps identity is nothing more than accumulated memory and if those memories are removed, reordered or misunderstood, the person experiencing them may completely misunderstand the nature of their own existence.

I’m the filmmaker, so this is obviously self-promotion, but what I’m actually curious about is interpretation rather than just getting people to click it.

## 5. How faithful does an adaptation actually need to be? - The Odyssey and Wuthering Heights

**Score:** 1
**Body:** With the recent success and discourse surrounding The Odyssey, I've been thinking a lot about the nature of text-to-film adaptations. Particularly, the expectations academics and general audiences alike place on cinema when adapting classic literature. Emily Wilson's recent pieces about The Odyssey have inspired me to talk about Nolan's take on Homer's poem. In the same vein, Fennell was blasted this past February for desecrating Bront*ë*'s Wuthering Heights for obvious reasons, in my opinion. For me, The Odyssey largely works as a filmed adaptation whereas Wuthering Heights misses the mark quite deeply. And I wanted to compare these two approaches to explore the limits of film adaptations and what a director's responsibility is to the source material.  

Generally, what interests me isn't really whether a filmmaker should recreate a book scene-for-scene. I think adaptation requires transformation because traversing from medium to medium necessitates artistic concessions. The more interesting question is whether a filmmaker can radically reinterpret a text while still preserving what I’m calling its “emotional truth.” And an "emotional truth" can vary from person to person, but as long as it preserves the essence of the novel or remains in dialogue with it. 

That’s ultimately why The Odyssey worked so well for me. Nolan obviously makes enormous changes and concessions, but I felt that his film was still in conversation with the ideas and emotional core of Homer’s poem. It felt like Nolan was \**interpreting* the text rather than simply borrowing its characters and imagery.

I had almost the exact opposite reaction to Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights. Full disclosure: I have not read Brontë’s novel, so I don't want to pretend I have the authority to make definitive claims about the text. I have seen William Wyler's much more faithful adaptation, and I've read extensively about the novel's themes, characters, and relationship to Victorian ideas about love and passion. So I recognize that this weakens my argument somewhat, particularly when I'm criticizing Fennell's fidelity to a book I haven't personally read.

But even with that caveat, I found myself fascinated by the larger question: when does creative liberty become a rejection of the source material rather than an interpretation of it? To me, the mere addition of a sexual relationship between Heathcliff and Catherine completely eschews the nature of the relationship that Brontë originally wrote about. So many of the novel's themes hinge on a non-sexual dynamic and the unspoken passions. Rejecting that entirely without the weight of what a sexual affair actually means completely dismisses the intentions of Brontë. 

Can a filmmaker change almost everything about a classic text and still capture what made it meaningful? Does “faithfulness” even matter if the adaptation discovers something genuinely new? Or is there some essential emotional or thematic truth that a filmmaker has a responsibility to preserve?

I wrote a piece thinking through those questions through The Odyssey and Wuthering Heights. I'd love to hear how you all think about adaptation, particularly from people who have actually read both texts.
